Welcome back, Alan. You've now completed all of Topic 1 — a thorough
journey through the Pre-Socratics, from Thales through the Atomists.
This lesson picks up exactly where that left off, moving into Topic 2:
Socrates and the Sophists.

Sophists and Socrates

Lesson page created

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

After nine lessons' worth of cosmology and metaphysics, this lesson
marks the famous pivot — where philosophy turns from the heavens to the
human being. Here's what this lesson covers:

1.  **2.1 The Sophists** — who they were and why relativism genuinely
    threatened philosophy
2.  **2.2 Socrates vs. the Sophists** — what it means to know that you
    don't know
3.  **2.3 The Socratic Method** — how elenchus works, with a deep dive
    into the Euthyphro

By the end, you'll have a firm grip on what Socrates was actually doing
— and why it was controversial enough to get him killed.

# Course Syllabus: History of Western Philosophy

## Topic 0: Course Introduction

An orientation to the journey ahead — what philosophy is, why its
history matters, and how the topics in this course build on one another
across twenty-five centuries.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)0.1

Roadmap introduction

What philosophy asks, why its history is the best way to learn it, and
how each era sets up the next

## Topic 1: The Pre-Socratics

Philosophy begins not with answers but with a radical change in the kind
of question being asked — replacing mythological explanation with
reasoned inquiry into the nature of reality.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)1.1

Why philosophy? The leap from myth to reason

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)1.2

Thales and Anaximander

the first cosmologists

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)1.3

Pythagoras

number as the key to reality

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)1.4

Heraclitus

everything flows

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)1.5

Parmenides

change is impossible

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)1.6

Zeno's paradoxes

motion, infinity, and the limits of reason

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)1.7

Democritus and the atomists

matter at the bottom

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)1.8

The Pre-Socratic legacy

what questions they left behind

## Topic 2: Socrates and the Sophists

The focus of philosophy shifts from the cosmos to the human being — from
"what is the world made of?" to "how should I live?"

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)2.1

The Sophists

teaching virtue for pay

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)2.2

Socrates vs. the Sophists

is virtue teachable?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)2.3

The Socratic method (elenchus)

dialogue as philosophy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)2.4

Socratic ethics

the unexamined life

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)2.5

The trial and death of Socrates

## Topic 3: Plato

Plato is the first systematic philosopher and the pivot around which all
of Western philosophy rotates.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.1

Plato's dialogues as philosophical form

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.2

The Theory of Forms

the real world behind appearances

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.3

The Allegory of the Cave

knowledge and education

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.4

The Divided Line

levels of reality and knowing

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.5

The soul

immortality, recollection, and the tripartite structure

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.6

The Republic I

justice in the soul and the city

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.7

The Republic II

the philosopher-king and the ideal city

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.8

The Republic III

critiques of democracy, poetry, and the myth of Er

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.9

The Symposium

love, beauty, and the ascent to the Form of the Good

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)3.10

Plato's legacy

problems he leaves open

## Topic 4: Aristotle

Aristotle is philosophy's great synthesizer and systematizer — he
simultaneously dismantles Plato's world of separate Forms and rebuilds a
richer account of substance, nature, knowledge, and the good life.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.1

Aristotle vs. Plato

why Forms must come down to earth

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.2

Logic

the Organon and the syllogism

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.3

Categories and substance

the basic structure of reality

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.4

Hylomorphism

form and matter

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.5

The four causes

explaining why things are as they are

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.6

Potentiality and actuality

change explained

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.7

Epistemology

how we come to know

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.8

The Nicomachean Ethics I

eudaimonia and the function argument

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.9

The Nicomachean Ethics II

virtue as the golden mean

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.10

The Nicomachean Ethics III

friendship, pleasure, and the contemplative life

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.11

Politics

the polis and the political animal

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)4.12

Aristotle's legacy

the Philosopher who ruled the Middle Ages

## Topic 5: Hellenistic Philosophy

After Alexander the Great, three great schools emerge to answer the
question pressing on every individual: how do I live well in a world I
cannot control?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)5.1

The Hellenistic context

philosophy as therapy for a troubled world

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)5.2

Epicurus

pleasure, atoms, and the art of tranquility

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)5.3

Epicurean physics

atoms and the clinamen

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)5.4

Stoicism

logos, fate, and what is up to us

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)5.5

Stoic ethics

living according to nature

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)5.6

Pyrrho and Academic Skepticism

suspending judgment

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)5.7

Hellenistic legacy

how these schools shaped Roman thought and beyond

## Topic 6: Medieval Philosophy

Medieval philosophy is where some of philosophy's sharpest problems
(universals, existence, necessary being, reason vs. revelation) were
fought over with great precision.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.1

Augustine

faith seeking understanding

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.2

The problem of universals

realism vs. nominalism

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.3

Anselm and the ontological argument

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.4

Islamic philosophy

Al-Kindi, Avicenna, Averroes

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.5

Jewish philosophy

Maimonides and negative theology

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.6

Thomas Aquinas I

faith and reason in harmony

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.7

Thomas Aquinas II

the five ways and natural theology

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.8

Thomas Aquinas III

natural law and ethics

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)6.9

William of Ockham

nominalism and the limits of reason

## Topic 7: Renaissance and Early Modern Philosophy

The Renaissance dissolves the medieval synthesis, and a new science of
nature forces a complete rethinking of what knowledge is and how to get
it.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.1

The Renaissance context

humanism and the recovery of antiquity

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.2

Machiavelli

politics without morality

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.3

The scientific revolution and its philosophical shock

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.4

Francis Bacon

the inductive method and the reform of learning

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.5

Descartes I

radical doubt and the cogito

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.6

Descartes II

mind, body, and the existence of God

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.7

Descartes III

the legacy and problems of Cartesian dualism

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.8

Spinoza

one substance, God-or-Nature

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)7.9

Leibniz

monads, pre-established harmony, and the best of all possible worlds

## Topic 8: The British Empiricists

Where the rationalists grounded knowledge in innate ideas and pure
reason, the empiricists insist that all knowledge comes from experience.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.1

What is empiricism? The core commitment

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.2

Locke I

ideas, primary and secondary qualities

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.3

Locke II

personal identity, substance, and what we cannot know

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.4

Locke III

political philosophy and the social contract

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.5

Berkeley

to be is to be perceived

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.6

Hume I

impressions, ideas, and the limits of knowledge

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.7

Hume II

causation — habit, not necessity

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.8

Hume III

the self as bundle of perceptions

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.9

Hume IV

religion, miracles, and the design argument

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)8.10

Hume's problem of induction

the deepest challenge

## Topic 9: Kant

Kant is the hinge of modern philosophy — woken by Hume's skepticism, he
attempts a complete restructuring of epistemology.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.1

The Copernican revolution in philosophy

what Kant reverses

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.2

Analytic and synthetic, a priori and a posteriori

Kant's key distinctions

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.3

The Transcendental Aesthetic

space and time as forms of intuition

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.4

The Transcendental Analytic

the categories of understanding

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.5

The Transcendental Dialectic

the limits of reason

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.6

Phenomena and noumena

things as they appear vs. things in themselves

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.7

Kant's ethics I

the good will and the categorical imperative

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.8

Kant's ethics II

humanity as end in itself and the kingdom of ends

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.9

The Critique of Judgment

beauty, sublimity, and teleology

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)9.10

Kant's legacy and immediate reception

## Topic 10: German Idealism and Hegel

Kant's successors eliminate the mysterious "thing-in-itself" by making
reality fully rational and fully knowable — leading to Hegel and his
dialectical account of history, Spirit, and freedom.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.1

Post-Kantian idealism

Fichte and the absolute ego

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.2

Schelling

nature as visible spirit

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.3

Hegel's dialectic

thesis, antithesis, synthesis — and what it really means

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.4

The Phenomenology of Spirit I

consciousness and self-consciousness

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.5

The Phenomenology of Spirit II

the master-slave dialectic

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.6

Hegel's logic

being, nothing, and becoming

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.7

Hegel's philosophy of history

the rational is actual

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.8

Hegel's political philosophy

the rational state

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)10.9

Hegel's influence

why he polarizes everything that follows

## Topic 11: 19th-Century Responses

Hegel's grand system provoked four of the nineteenth century's most
important philosophers into furious, contrasting responses.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.1

Schopenhauer

the world as will and representation

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.2

Schopenhauer

art, asceticism, and the denial of will

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.3

Kierkegaard

the leap of faith and the three stages of existence

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.4

Kierkegaard

subjectivity, anxiety, and authentic selfhood

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.5

Marx I

historical materialism and the critique of Hegel

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.6

Marx II

alienation, capitalism, and the critique of political economy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.7

Nietzsche I

the death of God and nihilism

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.8

Nietzsche II

master and slave morality

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.9

Nietzsche III

the will to power, eternal recurrence, and the Übermensch

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)11.10

Nietzsche IV

perspectivism and the critique of truth

## Topic 12: Analytic Philosophy

At the turn of the twentieth century, a new style of philosophy emerges
that turns away from grand metaphysical systems toward the logical
analysis of language and thought.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)12.1

What is analytic philosophy? A new philosophical method

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)12.2

Frege

logic, sense, and reference

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)12.3

Russell I

logicism and Principia Mathematica

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)12.4

Russell II

descriptions, logical atomism, and the philosophy of language

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)12.5

G.E. Moore

common sense and the naturalistic fallacy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)12.6

Early Wittgenstein

the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)12.7

Logical positivism

the Vienna Circle and the verification principle

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)12.8

The unraveling of logical positivism

Quine and Popper

## Topic 13: Continental Philosophy

A parallel tradition turns to lived experience, embodiment, and the
question of being itself — Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre, de Beauvoir,
Merleau-Ponty, and Levinas.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)13.1

What is continental philosophy? A different approach to the same
questions

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)13.2

Husserl

intentionality and the phenomenological method

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)13.3

Heidegger I

Being and Time — the question of Being

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)13.6

## Topic 14: Later Analytic Philosophy

The late Wittgenstein's rejection of his own early theory transforms
analytic philosophy — while Quine, Rawls, and philosophy of mind take it
in new directions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)14.1

Late Wittgenstein

meaning as use

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)14.2

Language-games, family resemblance, and following a rule

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)14.3

Ordinary language philosophy

Austin and Ryle

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)14.4

Quine

the indeterminacy of translation and the web of belief

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)14.5

Philosophy of mind

functionalism and the hard problem

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)14.6

Rawls

A Theory of Justice and the veil of ignorance

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)14.7

Nozick

libertarianism and the minimal state

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)14.8

Philosophy of science

Kuhn, Popper, and scientific revolutions

## Topic 15: Postmodernism and Contemporary Thought

Foucault, Derrida, Lyotard, and Rorty each question the very foundations
of the Western philosophical project — universal reason, objective
truth, and grand historical narratives.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.1

What is postmodernism? The critique of the Enlightenment project

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.2

Foucault I

knowledge, power, and archaeology of discourse

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.3

Foucault II

discipline, surveillance, and the genealogy of the subject

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.4

Foucault III

sexuality, the care of the self, and ethics

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.5

Derrida

deconstruction and the instability of meaning

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.6

Lyotard

the postmodern condition and the end of grand narratives

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.7

Rorty

pragmatism, irony, and the end of epistemology

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.8

Contemporary threads

feminism, critical theory, and analytic-continental rapprochement

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.9

Where does Western philosophy stand today?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)15.10

your own philosophical position
